title: Peace on the messengers
hook: glory to your Lord, peace on the messengers, praise to Allah (37:180–182)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yunus again, and your line was glorifying got him out. Did you practice a little glorifying while nothing was wrong? Today, the last three verses of As-Saffat. Day five hundred fifty-four.

Some songs have a refrain you start waiting for. The verse changes, the story moves on, and then the chorus comes back and you can almost sing it before it arrives. Surah As-Saffat has one. It tells story after story of prophets, and after several of them the same short line returns, like a bell: peace be on him. And then, at the very end, the refrain opens up to include every messenger at once, and the surah closes with three lines some Muslims use to close a gathering.

Go back through As-Saffat and listen for it. After Nuh's story: peace be on Nuh among the worlds. After Ibrahim's: peace be on Ibrahim. After Musa and Harun's: peace be on Musa and Harun. After Ilyas: peace be on Il-yasin. Each time, the Arabic begins salamun 'ala, peace upon. Four of the stories end that way, in peace, however hard they were. Then, the surah's last three verses. First: glory to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. In the verse, that clears away every wrong picture of Allah. Second, Pickthall: "And peace be unto those sent (to warn). And praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds!" Now the refrain isn't for one prophet. It's for all of them, the named and the unnamed, everyone ever sent. And the last word goes back to the opening of al-Fatiha: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi'l-'alamin, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. So the surah ends with three moves: glory, peace, praise. Glory says what Allah is above. Peace blesses those who carried His message. Praise says where everything belongs. Commentators, including Ibn Kathir, mention an early saying that whoever wants their reward measured out in full should end their gathering with these verses. Its chain is discussed. Some Muslims recite them at the end of a lesson, a dinner, a meeting. Ending a conversation by wishing peace on every messenger who ever lived is not a bad way to leave a room.
screen: `PRAISE TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to end the day with these three, so rehearse them now. Sit and breathe. On one breath, think glory: the verse says God is beyond whatever is pictured. On the next, think peace: on every messenger, every person who ever carried something true to people who didn't want it. On the next, think praise: where everything belongs. If you pray, you can say the three verses in Arabic or in your own language. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Salamun, peace, the refrain that follows each prophet's story in As-Saffat, and widens at the end to bless every messenger. Today's word.
Your line: glory, peace, praise. Tonight, before you sleep, or at the end of a gathering, close with the three: glory, peace, praise. Day five hundred fifty-four.

fork.setup: all through As-Saffat, peace is wished on one prophet at a time. at the very end, who does the refrain include?
fork.reveal: all the messengers, named and unnamed, between glory to Allah and praise to the Lord of the Worlds.

what it means: the surah's refrain of peace on each prophet widens to all of them, framed by glory and praise.
what a scholar hears: salamun 'ala recurs at 37:79, 109, 120 and 130 before 37:181; Ibn Kathir cites an early report about ending gatherings with 37:180–182.
